claim: Chytrids span some of the deepest fungal Phyla.
source: Zoosporic fungi, commonly referred to as 'chytrids', span some of the deepest fungal Phyla and comprise much of the undescribed environmental fungal DNA diversity in aquatic ecosystems (James et al., 2006; Richards et al., 2012; Powell and Letcher, 2014; Grossart et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Chytrids comprise much of the undescribed environmental fungal DNA diversity in aquatic ecosystems.
source: Zoosporic fungi, commonly referred to as 'chytrids', span some of the deepest fungal Phyla and comprise much of the undescribed environmental fungal DNA diversity in aquatic ecosystems (James et al., 2006; Richards et al., 2012; Powell and Letcher, 2014; Grossart et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Many chytrids are saprophytes or parasites of photosynthetic organisms and actively shuttle carbon to higher trophic levels.
source: Many chytrids are saprophytes or parasites of photosynthetic organisms and actively shuttle carbon to higher trophic levels (Kagami et al., 2014; Grossart et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis is a frog-killing chytrid.
source: Other chytrids are animal parasites, including the Batrachochytrium genus that includes the frog-killing B. dendrobatidis (Longcore et al., 1999) and salamander-killing B. salamandrivorans that are devastating global amphibian populations (Martel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans is a salamander-killing chytrid.
source: Other chytrids are animal parasites, including the Batrachochytrium genus that includes the frog-killing B. dendrobatidis (Longcore et al., 1999) and salamander-killing B. salamandrivorans that are devastating global amphibian populations (Martel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Batrachochytrium species are devastating global amphibian populations.
source: Other chytrids are animal parasites, including the Batrachochytrium genus that includes the frog-killing B. dendrobatidis (Longcore et al., 1999) and salamander-killing B. salamandrivorans that are devastating global amphibian populations (Martel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Chytrids have retained ancestral cellular features shared by animal cells and amoebae.
source: Chytrids are unique in that they have retained ancestral cellular features, shared by animal cells and amoebae, while also having fungal features.
evidence: General statement about chytrid biology based on established knowledge

claim: Chytrids begin their life as motile zoospores that lack a cell wall.
source: For example, chytrids begin their life as motile zoospores that lack a cell wall, swim with a single posterior cilium nucleated from a centriole, and crawl across surfaces (Fuller, 1976; Sparrow, 1960; Deacon and Saxena, 1997; Held, 1975; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Chytrid zoospores swim with a single posterior cilium nucleated from a centriole.
source: For example, chytrids begin their life as motile zoospores that lack a cell wall, swim with a single posterior cilium nucleated from a centriole, and crawl across surfaces (Fuller, 1976; Sparrow, 1960; Deacon and Saxena, 1997; Held, 1975; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Chytrid zoospores crawl across surfaces.
source: For example, chytrids begin their life as motile zoospores that lack a cell wall, swim with a single posterior cilium nucleated from a centriole, and crawl across surfaces (Fuller, 1976; Sparrow, 1960; Deacon and Saxena, 1997; Held, 1975; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Later life cycle stages of chytrids exhibit fungal characteristics including the formation of chitinous cell walls.
source: Later life cycle stages exhibit fungal characteristics including the formation of chitinous cell walls, the growth of hyphal-like structures, and the development of a sporangium (sporangiogenesis); see Figure 1.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1 which illustrates the life cycle stages

claim: Chytrid zoosporogenesis involves multiple rounds of mitosis without cytokinesis to create a multi-nuclear coenocyte.
source: Chytrid zoosporogenesis involves multiple rounds of mitosis without cytokinesis to create a multi-nuclear coenocyte, followed by cellularization to form zoospores with a single nucleus.
evidence: General description of chytrid developmental biology based on established knowledge

claim: Chytrid zoosporogenesis is followed by cellularization to form zoospores with a single nucleus.
source: Chytrid zoosporogenesis involves multiple rounds of mitosis without cytokinesis to create a multi-nuclear coenocyte, followed by cellularization to form zoospores with a single nucleus.
evidence: General description of chytrid developmental biology based on established knowledge

claim: The formation of a multinuclear compartment followed by cellularization is reminiscent of development in flies, amoeba, and protozoa.
source: The formation of a multinuclear compartment followed by cellularization is reminiscent of development in flies (e.g. Drosophila), amoeba (e.g. Physarum), and protozoa (e.g. Plasmodium).
evidence: Comparative statement drawing on established knowledge of development in different organisms

claim: The major bottleneck to studying chytrids in molecular detail has been the lack of a model organism with tools for genetic transformation.
source: The major bottleneck to studying chytrids in molecular detail has been the lack of a model organism with tools for genetic transformation.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field prior to this work

claim: This study describes successful adaptation of Agrobacterium-mediated transformation to generate reliable and stable genetic transformation of Spizellomyces punctatus.
source: Here, we describe the successful adaptation of Agrobacterium-mediated transformation to generate reliable and stable genetic transformation of the soil chytrid Spizellomyces punctatus.
evidence: Primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: Spizellomyces undergoes multiple rounds of synchronous nuclear division.
source: We show that the chytrid undergoes multiple rounds of synchronous nuclear division, followed by cellularization, to create and release many daughter 'zoospores'.
evidence: Primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3

claim: Spizellomyces undergoes cellularization to create and release many daughter zoospores.
source: We show that the chytrid undergoes multiple rounds of synchronous nuclear division, followed by cellularization, to create and release many daughter 'zoospores'.
evidence: Primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5

claim: Spizellomyces zoospores crawl using actin-mediated cell migration.
source: The zoospores, akin to animal cells, crawl using actin-mediated cell migration.
evidence: Primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4

claim: After forming a cell wall, polymerized actin in Spizellomyces reorganizes into fungal-like cortical patches and cables.
source: After forming a cell wall, polymerized actin reorganizes into fungal-like cortical patches and cables that extend into hyphal-like structures.
evidence: Primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5

claim: Actin perinuclear shells form each cell cycle in Spizellomyces.
source: Actin perinuclear shells form each cell cycle and polygonal territories emerge during cellularization.
evidence: Primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5

claim: Polygonal territories emerge during cellularization in Spizellomyces.
source: Actin perinuclear shells form each cell cycle and polygonal territories emerge during cellularization.
evidence: Primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5

claim: Spizellomyces punctatus produces globular zoospores that are 3-5 µm in size.
source: The chytrid produces globular zoospores (3–5 µm) that swim with a motile cilium (20–24 µm).
evidence: Measurement reported in Figure 1 caption

claim: Spizellomyces zoospores swim with a motile cilium that is 20-24 µm in length.
source: The chytrid produces globular zoospores (3–5 µm) that swim with a motile cilium (20–24 µm).
evidence: Measurement reported in Figure 1 caption

claim: The start of encystment in Spizellomyces occurs before 1 hr when the cilium retracts by a lash-around mechanism.
source: The start of encystment (before 1 hr) occurs when the cilium retracts by a lash-around mechanism, followed by formation of cell wall (Koch, 1968).
evidence: Timing data from this study combined with citation to mechanism from Koch, 1968

claim: Spizellomyces cysts germinate and form a single germ tube at 1-3 hr.
source: The cyst then germinates and forms a single germ tube (at 1–3 hr) that later expands and branches into a rhizoidal system.
evidence: Timing data from experimental observations in this study

claim: The first mitotic event in Spizellomyces usually correlates with the ramification of rhizoids from the germ tube.
source: The first mitotic event (at 8–12 hr) usually correlates with the ramification of rhizoids from the germ tube.
evidence: Observation from experimental data in this study

claim: The first mitotic event in Spizellomyces occurs at 8-12 hr.
source: The first mitotic event (at 8–12 hr) usually correlates with the ramification of rhizoids from the germ tube.
evidence: Timing data from experimental observations in this study

claim: Spizellomyces sporangia can undergo a total of five to eight synchronous mitotic cycles.
source: There can be a total of five to eight synchronous mitotic cycles as each sporangium develops a branched rhizoid system with subsporangial swelling in the main rhizoid.
evidence: Quantitative data from experimental observations in this study

claim: Ciliogenesis likely occurs before cellularization in Spizellomyces as in other chytrids.
source: Ciliogenesis likely occurs before cellularization as in other chytrids (Renaud and Swift, 1964).
evidence: Inference based on citation to other chytrids

claim: Zoospores escape the Spizellomyces sporangium through discharge papillae at 20-30 hr.
source: Once cellularization is complete and environmental conditions are favorable, the zoospores will escape the sporangium through the discharge papillae (at 20–30 hr).
evidence: Timing data from experimental observations in this study

claim: Agrobacterium tumefaciens normally induces plant tumors by injecting and integrating T-DNA from a Ti-plasmid into the plant genome.
source: The plant pathogen Agrobacterium tumefaciens normally induces plant tumors by injecting and integrating a segment of transfer DNA (T-DNA) from a tumor-inducing plasmid (Ti-plasmid) into the plant genome.
evidence: Established knowledge about Agrobacterium biology

claim: Agrobacterium-mediated transformation has been adapted for transformation of diverse animals and fungi.
source: Because Agrobacterium-mediated transformation has been adapted for transformation of diverse animals and fungi (Bundock et al., 1995; Kunik et al., 2001; Covert et al., 2001; Ianiri et al., 2017; Vieira and Camilo, 2011), we chose to use this system in Spizellomyces punctatus.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: 200 mg/L Hygromycin resulted in complete absence of Spizellomyces growth after 6 days of incubation at 30°C.
source: Although Geneticin (G418), Puromycin, and Phleomycin D10 (Zeocin) did not inhibit growth up to 800 mg/L, we determined that 200 mg/L Hygromycin and 800 mg/L Nourseothricin (CloNAT) resulted in complete absence of growth after 6 days of incubation at 30°C.
evidence: Experimental result from drug testing in this study

claim: 800 mg/L Nourseothricin (CloNAT) resulted in complete absence of Spizellomyces growth after 6 days of incubation at 30°C.
source: Although Geneticin (G418), Puromycin, and Phleomycin D10 (Zeocin) did not inhibit growth up to 800 mg/L, we determined that 200 mg/L Hygromycin and 800 mg/L Nourseothricin (CloNAT) resulted in complete absence of growth after 6 days of incubation at 30°C.
evidence: Experimental result from drug testing in this study

claim: Geneticin (G418), Puromycin, and Phleomycin D10 (Zeocin) did not inhibit Spizellomyces growth up to 800 mg/L.
source: Although Geneticin (G418), Puromycin, and Phleomycin D10 (Zeocin) did not inhibit growth up to 800 mg/L, we determined that 200 mg/L Hygromycin and 800 mg/L Nourseothricin (CloNAT) resulted in complete absence of growth after 6 days of incubation at 30°C.
evidence: Experimental result from drug testing in this study

claim: Spizellomyces HSP70 and H2B promoters resulted in resistance to Hygromycin in yeast.
source: We confirmed that Spizellomyces HSP70 and H2B promoters resulted in resistance to Hygromycin as well as measurable GFP fluorescence in yeast via flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and microscopy.
evidence: Experimental result from yeast testing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Spizellomyces HSP70 and H2B promoters resulted in measurable GFP fluorescence in yeast.
source: We confirmed that Spizellomyces HSP70 and H2B promoters resulted in resistance to Hygromycin as well as measurable GFP fluorescence in yeast via flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and microscopy.
evidence: Experimental result from yeast testing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: None of the GFP transformants of Spizellomyces exhibited green fluorescence above background.
source: Although Hygromycin-resistant, none of the GFP transformants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) exhibited green fluorescence above background.
evidence: Experimental observation from transformation experiments

claim: GFP lack of fluorescence in Spizellomyces is likely due to GFP misfolding.
source: This has been seen in other emerging model systems (i.e. choanoflagellate Salpingoeca Booth et al., 2018) and is likely due to GFP misfolding.
evidence: Inference based on citation to similar observation in another organism

claim: When GFP was replaced by tdTomato in Spizellomyces, transformants exhibited both Hygromycin resistance and cytoplasmic fluorescence.
source: When GFP was replaced by tdTomato, we obtained transformants that exhibited both Hygromycin resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and cytoplasmic fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and 2

claim: mClover3, mCitrine, and mCerulean3 are functional in Spizellomyces.
source: Further tests with other fluorescent protein fusions showed that mClover3, mCitrine, and mCerulean3 are functional in Spizellomyces (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Chytrid transformation with H2B-tdTomato resulted in bright nuclear localization of fluorescence.
source: Chytrid transformation with H2B-tdTomato resulted in bright nuclear localization of fluorescence when compared to cytoplasmic tdTomato (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2B

claim: The presence of the T-DNA in the transformants was confirmed using PCR for hph and H2B-tdTomato.
source: The presence of the T-DNA (total size of 4280 bp) in the transformants was confirmed using PCR for hph and H2B-tdTomato (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and through Southern blot analysis of hph (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2C

claim: Southern blot analysis confirmed the presence of T-DNA in the transformants.
source: The presence of the T-DNA (total size of 4280 bp) in the transformants was confirmed using PCR for hph and H2B-tdTomato (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and through Southern blot analysis of hph (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2C

claim: The results were consistent with random, single T-DNA genomic integration events in each transformant.
source: The results were consistent with random, single T-DNA genomic integration events in each transformant.
evidence: Interpretation of Southern blot and PCR data

claim: In three of the four transformants (EM20C-1, 2, 3), the T-DNA LB was located within 200 bp upstream of the transcription start site of a gene.
source: In three of the four transformants (EM20C-1, 2, 3), the T-DNA LB was located within 200 bp upstream of the transcription start site (TSS) of a gene (SPPG_04375 an M48 peptidase, SPPG_03425 an adenine nucleotide hydrolase, and SPPG_02523 a PHO-like cyclin, respectively).
evidence: Experimental result from inverse PCR and sequencing

claim: For strain EM20C-4, the LB T-DNA was inserted 844 bp from the closest TSS.
source: Last, for strain EM20C-4, the LB T-DNA was inserted 844 bp from the closest TSS (SPPG_08788 a hypothetical protein).
evidence: Experimental result from inverse PCR and sequencing

claim: Strains EM20C-2, 3, 4 showed similar and unimodal levels of tdTomato fluorescence at the population level.
source: The data show that strains EM20C-2, 3, 4 showed similar and unimodal levels of tdTomato fluorescence at the population level, despite the different sites of genomic integration.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Strain EM20C-1 exhibits bimodal gene expression with the top mode identical to other transformants and the bottom mode at half the intensity.
source: The exception is EM20C-1, which exhibits bimodal gene expression: the top mode is identical to the other transformants, but the bottom mode is half the intensity.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The transformants had transgenerational stability when passaged in non-selective medium for several weeks followed by a challenge in selective medium.
source: Last, we established that the transformants had transgenerational stability by passaging them in non-selective medium for several weeks, followed by a challenge in selective medium (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2D

claim: Spizellomyces zoospores have a single nucleus.
source: Our results show that zoospores have a single nucleus, they retract their flagellum and encyst in less than 1 hr, the germ tube emerges at ∼1−3 hr, the first mitotic event (i.e. one nucleus to two nuclei) occurs at ∼8−12 hr, and sporangia develop and undergo 5–8 mitotic cycles in less than 30 hr before completing their life cycles and releasing 32–256 zoospores; see Figure 2—video 1.
evidence: Experimental observation from live-cell imaging

claim: Spizellomyces zoospores retract their flagellum and encyst in less than 1 hr.
source: Our results show that zoospores have a single nucleus, they retract their flagellum and encyst in less than 1 hr, the germ tube emerges at ∼1−3 hr, the first mitotic event (i.e. one nucleus to two nuclei) occurs at ∼8−12 hr, and sporangia develop and undergo 5–8 mitotic cycles in less than 30 hr before completing their life cycles and releasing 32–256 zoospores; see Figure 2—video 1.
evidence: Experimental observation from live-cell imaging

claim: Spizellomyces sporangia develop and undergo 5-8 mitotic cycles in less than 30 hr before releasing 32-256 zoospores.
source: Our results show that zoospores have a single nucleus, they retract their flagellum and encyst in less than 1 hr, the germ tube emerges at ∼1−3 hr, the first mitotic event (i.e. one nucleus to two nuclei) occurs at ∼8−12 hr, and sporangia develop and undergo 5–8 mitotic cycles in less than 30 hr before completing their life cycles and releasing 32–256 zoospores; see Figure 2—video 1.
evidence: Experimental observation from live-cell imaging

claim: The average cell cycle period in Spizellomyces was approximately 150 min.
source: We found that the average cell cycle period was ∼150 min and that each wave of nuclear division was completed within 1 min (Figure 3B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3B

claim: Each wave of nuclear division in Spizellomyces was completed within 1 min.
source: We found that the average cell cycle period was ∼150 min and that each wave of nuclear division was completed within 1 min (Figure 3B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3B

claim: All measurable mitotic events in Spizellomyces occurred within 5 min, or less than 3.3% of the cell cycle period.
source: In addition, by following the compaction and localization of H2B-tdTomato we show that all measurable mitotic events occurred within 5 min, or less than 3.3% of the cell cycle period (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Spizellomyces is mitotically inactive in its early life cycle (zoospore and germination stages).
source: Altogether, these results show that Spizellomyces is mitotically inactive in its early life cycle (zoospore and germination stages) but, once committed, the cell cycle is fast and nuclear divisions within each sporangium are highly synchronous; see Table 1.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations from live-cell imaging

claim: Once committed, the Spizellomyces cell cycle is fast and nuclear divisions within each sporangium are highly synchronous.
source: Altogether, these results show that Spizellomyces is mitotically inactive in its early life cycle (zoospore and germination stages) but, once committed, the cell cycle is fast and nuclear divisions within each sporangium are highly synchronous; see Table 1.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations from live-cell imaging and comparison in Table 1

claim: Spizellomyces has homologs of WASP (SPPG_00537) and SCAR/WAVE (SPPG_02302).
source: Spizellomyces has homologs of WASP (SPPG_00537), SCAR/WAVE (SPPG_02302), and its zoospores are proficient crawlers.
evidence: Genomic analysis identifying gene homologs

claim: Spizellomyces zoospores are proficient crawlers.
source: Spizellomyces has homologs of WASP (SPPG_00537), SCAR/WAVE (SPPG_02302), and its zoospores are proficient crawlers.
evidence: Observation from experimental work

claim: LifeAct is a 17 amino acid peptide that binds specifically to polymerized actin in a wide variety of cell types.
source: LifeAct is a 17 amino acid peptide that binds specifically to polymerized actin in a wide variety of cell types, such as actin patches and cables in yeast and actin-filled protrusions of crawling animal cells (Riedl et al., 2008; Belin et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge about LifeAct supported by citations

claim: LifeAct-tdTomato fusion localization nearly perfectly correlated with phalloidin intensities in fixed Spizellomyces cells.
source: Because the LifeAct fusion localization nearly perfectly correlated with phalloidin intensities in fixed cells, but the hph fusion did not, we presume that this fluorescence represents polymerized actin.
evidence: Experimental comparison shown in Figure 4

claim: Spizellomyces experiments revealed an actin cytoskeleton distributed primarily between cortical patches and linear structures that resemble the actin cables of other fungal species.
source: Our experiments revealed an actin cytoskeleton distributed primarily between cortical patches and linear structures that resemble the actin cables of other fungal species (Figure 5A).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5A

claim: Transient perinuclear polymerized actin shells were detected in Spizellomyces with a period similar to mitotic events.
source: We also detected transient perinuclear polymerized actin shells with a period similar to mitotic events (Figure 5B and Figure 5—video 1), which suggests a role for polymerized actin with nuclei during the cell cycle.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—video 1

claim: In late sporangiogenesis, polymerized actin delineated polygonal zoospore territories in Spizellomyces.
source: In late sporangiogenesis, polymerized actin delineated polygonal zoospore territories (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5B-C

claim: Polygonal zoospore territories in Spizellomyces are reminiscent of epithelial cellularization seen during Drosophila embryogenesis when syncytial nuclei are encapsulated by cell membrane.
source: This is reminiscent of epithelial cellularization seen during Drosophila embryogenesis when syncytial nuclei are encapsulated by cell membrane.
evidence: Comparative statement drawing on established knowledge of Drosophila development

claim: This study reports stable and robust genetic transformation of the chytrid Spizellomyces punctatus.
source: Here, we report stable and robust genetic transformation of the chytrid Spizellomyces punctatus.
evidence: Summary statement of primary finding supported by experimental data throughout

claim: The divergent H2A/H2B promoter can simultaneously express Hygromycin resistance (hph) and a gene of interest throughout the chytrid life cycle.
source: We identified and tested native Spizellomyces promoters, including a divergent H2A/H2B promoter that can simultaneously express Hygromycin resistance (hph) and a gene of interest throughout the chytrid life cycle.
evidence: Experimental result from transformation and expression studies

claim: The H2A/H2B promoter design was used to express fluorescent proteins and resistance genes in Dikaryotic marine fungi.
source: This design was used to express fluorescent proteins and resistance genes in Dikaryotic marine fungi (data not shown), which suggests they should be useful for transforming other chytrids, such as the pathogenic Batrachochytrium.
evidence: Unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript

claim: Agrobacterium was previously used to transform the aquatic chytrid Blastocladiella emersonii.
source: Agrobacterium was previously used to transform the aquatic chytrid Blastocladiella emersonii (Vieira and Camilo, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Genetic transformation of Blastocladiella displayed a narrow window of gene expression and could only be detected at the zoosporic stage.
source: Unfortunately, genetic transformation of Blastocladiella displayed a narrow window of gene expression and could only be detected at the zoosporic stage.
evidence: Statement about limitations of prior work, based on published literature

claim: Agrobacterium T-DNA is often randomly integrated into the host chromosome as a single copy.
source: For example, Agrobacterium T-DNA is often randomly integrated into the host chromosome as a single copy and, if inserted within a gene, it will disrupt gene function and act as a mutagen (Gelvin, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge about Agrobacterium transformation supported by citation

claim: If Agrobacterium T-DNA is inserted within a gene, it will disrupt gene function and act as a mutagen.
source: For example, Agrobacterium T-DNA is often randomly integrated into the host chromosome as a single copy and, if inserted within a gene, it will disrupt gene function and act as a mutagen (Gelvin, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge about Agrobacterium transformation supported by citation

claim: Random insertional mutagenesis by Agrobacterium has been exploited for forward genetics in plants and fungi.
source: Random insertional mutagenesis by Agrobacterium has been exploited for forward genetics in plants and fungi (Alonso et al., 2003; Michielse et al., 2005; Idnurm et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to published literature

claim: In Fungi, Agrobacterium-mediated transformation has been used for targeted gene knock-outs by including 1-1.5 kb long flanking region of homology in the T-DNA to the desired target gene.
source: In Fungi, Agrobacterium-mediated transformation has also been used for targeted gene knock-outs by including 1–1.5 kb long, flanking region of homology in the T-DNA to the desired target gene (Frandsen et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to published literature

claim: The level of synchrony in Spizellomyces is similar to plasmodial nuclei in the amoeba Physarum polycephalum or syncytial nuclei during Drosophila development, where all nuclei divide within 2 min.
source: The level of synchrony is similar to plasmodial nuclei in the amoeba Physarum polycephalum or syncytial nuclei during Drosophila development, where all nuclei divide within 2 min (Deneke et al., 2016) (see Table 1).
evidence: Comparison to published data supported by citation and shown in Table 1

claim: Spizellomyces zoospores assemble thick actin cortices and build actin-filled protrusions during motility, similar to other chytrid species, animal cells, and amoebae.
source: By visualizing actin dynamics throughout the chytrid life cycle, we found that Spizellomyces zoospores assemble thick actin cortices and build actin-filled protrusions during motility, similar to other chytrid species (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b), animal cells, and amoebae.
evidence: Experimental observation compared to published literature

claim: Once Spizellomyces zoospores encyst, there is a drastic shift in actin cytoskeleton organization, in which the cortical shell of polymerized actin was replaced by dynamic puncta (actin patches).
source: Once the zoospores encyst, there is a drastic shift in actin cytoskeleton organization, in which the cortical shell of polymerized actin was replaced by dynamic puncta (actin patches), some of which are associated with actin cables that often extended into the germ tube or rhizoids.
evidence: Experimental observation from live-cell imaging

claim: In fungi, actin patches are associated with endocytosis and cell wall deposition, whereas actin cables are pathways for targeted delivery of exocytic vesicles.
source: This architecture is typical of fungi, where actin patches are associated with endocytosis and cell wall deposition, whereas actin cables are pathways for targeted delivery of exocytic vesicles (Lichius et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge about fungal actin supported by citation

claim: The biphasic actin distribution in Spizellomyces indicates that the actin cytoskeleton displays features that resemble those of both animal and fungal cells.
source: This biphasic actin distribution – an actin cortex and actin-filled protrusions in zoospores, and actin patches and cables in sporangia – indicates that, like its cell cycle regulatory network (Medina et al., 2016), the actin cytoskeleton of Spizellomyces displays features that resemble those of both animal and fungal cells.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental observations with reference to prior work

claim: Previous observations suggested that perinuclear actin shells of anaerobic chytrids were a fixation artifact.
source: Previous observations suggested that perinuclear actin shells of anaerobic chytrids were a fixation artifact (Li and Heath, 1994); however, our live cell data indicate that these are real, dynamic cellular structures that likely occur in many chytrids.
evidence: Comparison to published literature

claim: Live cell data from this study indicate that perinuclear actin shells are real, dynamic cellular structures that likely occur in many chytrids.
source: Previous observations suggested that perinuclear actin shells of anaerobic chytrids were a fixation artifact (Li and Heath, 1994); however, our live cell data indicate that these are real, dynamic cellular structures that likely occur in many chytrids.
evidence: Experimental observation from live-cell imaging

claim: Perinuclear actin shells are associated with nuclear lamina in animal cells, where they play a role in changing nuclear shape before and after mitosis.
source: Similar perinuclear actin shells are associated with nuclear lamina in animal cells, where they play a role in changing nuclear shape before and after mitosis (Clubb and Locke, 1998; Clubb and Locke, 1996 or when squeezing through narrow channels (Thiam et al., 2016).
evidence: Established knowledge about animal cells supported by citations

claim: Chytrids and other fungi have lost nuclear lamins.
source: Although chytrids and other fungi have lost nuclear lamins, it seems likely that Spizellomyces perinuclear actin shells are associated with changes in nuclear shape during the cell cycle.
evidence: Established knowledge about fungal cell biology

claim: Spizellomyces perinuclear actin shells are likely associated with changes in nuclear shape during the cell cycle.
source: Although chytrids and other fungi have lost nuclear lamins, it seems likely that Spizellomyces perinuclear actin shells are associated with changes in nuclear shape during the cell cycle.
evidence: Inference based on comparison to animal cells and experimental observations

claim: Polymerized actin is likely involved in the formation of zoospore polygonal territories before the formation of the cleavage planes during cellularization in Spizellomyces.
source: Finally, we showed that polymerized actin is likely involved in the formation of zoospore polygonal territories (Figure 5B) before the formation of the cleavage planes during cellularization.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5B

claim: Cellularization in Spizellomyces happens in a three-dimensional context within 3 hr.
source: In contrast to cellularization in Drosophila, which occurs at the surface of the embryo (i.e. two-dimensional cellularization), cellularization in Spizellomyces happens in a three-dimensional context within 3 hr.
evidence: Experimental observation and comparison to Drosophila

claim: The chytrid cellularization process is reminiscent of the polarized epithelium of the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: The chytrid cellularization process is reminiscent of the polarized epithelium of the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum (Dickinson et al., 2011; Dickinson et al., 2012) and the membrane invagination dynamics during cellularization in the ichthyosporean Sphaeroforma arctica, an unicellular relative of animals (Dudin et al., 2019).
